title: Avatarobots and the crisis of democracy: From bot armies to metaverse swarms
title-short: Avatarobots and the crisis of democracy
publisher: Alexander von Humboldt Institute for Internet
abstract: In this paper, we argue that immersive virtual reality environments, which we call the metaverse, can reproduce and intensify the risks social media platforms raise for democracies. At the center of our analysis are avatarobots, digital agents that resemble human beings, usually in their speech and behaviour, but sometimes also in their appearance, while operating partly or entirely without continuous direct human control. We examine how AI-powered avatarobots can fabricate synthetic majorities, simulate political agency, and distort the signals on which democratic legitimacy depends. To evaluate these risks, we develop the Principle of Accountable Free Expression (PAFE), structured around three criteria: authenticity, non-domination, and verifiability. These correspond to responsibility for speech, insulation from economic domination, and the verifiable origin of political communication. We use PAFE to analyse the democratic risks raised by avatarobots and to derive design and governance guidelines for immersive environments that aim to function as democratic public spheres.
aliases: Avatarobots and the crisis of democracy: From bot armies to metaverse swarms

title: Understanding responsibility in Responsible AI. Dianoetic virtues and the hard problem of context
abstract: Abstract During the last decade there has been burgeoning research concerning the ways in which we should think of and apply the concept of responsibility for Artificial Intelligence. Despite this conceptual richness, there is still a lack of consensus regarding what Responsible AI entails on both conceptual and practical levels. The aim of this paper is to connect the ethical dimension of responsibility in Responsible AI with Aristotelian virtue ethics, where notions of context and dianoetic virtues play a grounding role for the concept of moral responsibility. The paper starts by highlighting the important difficulties in assigning responsibility to either technologies themselves or to their developers. Top-down and bottom-up approaches to moral responsibility are then contrasted, as we explore how they could inform debates about Responsible AI. We highlight the limits of the former ethical approaches and build the case for classical Aristotelian virtue ethics. We show that two building blocks of Aristotle’s ethics, dianoetic virtues and the context of actions, although largely ignored in the literature, can shed light on how we could think of moral responsibility for both AI and humans. We end by exploring the practical implications of this particular understanding of moral responsibility along the triadic dimensions of ethics by design, ethics in design and ethics for designers.
aliases: Understanding responsibility in Responsible AI. Dianoetic virtues and the hard problem of context

title: Think: a compelling introduction to philosophy
edition: 1. publ. as an Oxford University Press paperback
abstract: This is a book about the big questions in life: knowledge, consciousness, fate, God, truth, goodness, justice. It is for anyone who thinks there are big questions lurking out there, but does not know how to approach them. Written by the author of the bestselling Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy, "Think" sets out to explain what they are and why they are important
